'''Natalie G. Ahn''' is a [[professor]] of [[chemistry]] and [[biochemistry]] at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]]. Her research is focused on understanding the mechanisms of cell signaling, with a speciality in [[phosphorylation]] and [[cancer]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2009.03.007 |pmid=19362540 |pmc=2735263 |title=Functional Proteomics Identifies Targets of Phosphorylation by B-Raf Signaling in Melanoma |journal=Molecular Cell |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=115–31 |year=2009 |last1=Old |first1=William M. |last2=Shabb |first2=John B. |last3=Houel |first3=Stephane |last4=Wang |first4=Hong |last5=Couts |first5=Kasey L. |last6=Yen |first6=Chia-yu |last7=Litman |first7=Elizabeth S. |last8=Croy |first8=Carrie H. |last9=Meyer-Arendt |first9=Karen |last10=Miranda |first10=Jose G. |last11=Brown |first11=Robert A. |last12=Witze |first12=Eric S. |last13=Schweppe |first13=Rebecca E. |last14=Resing |first14=Katheryn A. |last15=Ahn |first15=Natalie G. }}
* {{cite press release |date=April 17, 2009 |title=New Method For Detection Of Phosphoproteins Reveals Regulator Of Melanoma Invasion |website=ScienceDaily |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/04/090409134751.htm}}</ref> Ahn's work uses the tools of "classical chemistry" to work on understanding the genetic code and how genetics affects life processes.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Finding the Trees in the Proteomic Forest |last=Friedman |first=Roberta |date=January 2004 |journal=Genomics & Proteomics |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=38–40 }}</ref> She has been a professor at the University of Colorado at Boulder since 2003, where she is a distinguished professor.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.colorado.edu/biochemistry/natalie-ahn|title=Natalie Ahn|website=University of Colorado Boulder|date=9 October 2015 |access-date=September 20, 2018}}</ref> She was a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator between 1994 and 2014.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url = http://www.hhmi.org/scientists/natalie-g-ahn|title = Natalie G. Ahn, PhD|access-date = 15 January 2016|website = Howard Hughes Medical Institute}}</ref> In 2018, she was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and named a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name="nas2018">{{cite news|title=National Academy of Sciences Members and Foreign Associates Elected|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/May-1-2018-NAS-Election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180501225028/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/May-1-2018-NAS-Election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 1, 2018|access-date=12 May 2018|agency=National Academy of Sciences|date=1 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="AAAS">{{cite web |title=Newly Elected Fellows |url=https://members.amacad.org/content/members/newfellows.aspx?s=a |website=members.amacad.org |access-date=January 13, 2019 |archive-date=January 14, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190114210300/https://members.amacad.org/content/members/newfellows.aspx?s=a |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2021, Ahn was named to the ASBMB's first fellowship class.<ref>{{Cite web |title=First class |url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmb-today/people/042721/first-class |access-date=2026-10-09 |website=www.asbmb.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Biography ==
=== Past education, research, and awards ===
Ahn earned her [[bachelor's degree]] in chemistry from the [[University of Washington|University of Washington, Seattle]] in 1979.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.asbmb.org/asbmbtoday/201606/Features/Ahn/|title=Feature: Meet Natalie Ahn, ASBMB's incoming president|website=www.asbmb.org|access-date=2016-11-08}}</ref> Ahn conducted research in Lyle Jensen's lab, focusing on [[X-ray crystallography]].<ref name=":4" /> Her participation in this research aided in better understanding of protein folding and visualizing of the 3-D structure of proteins by using computational techniques with X-ray crystallography.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.washington.edu/research/pathbreakers/1943a.html|title=Molecular Anatomy: X-Ray Crystallography Helps Solve the Mystery of Protein Structure|website=www.washington.edu|access-date=2016-11-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150825084300/http://www.washington.edu/research/pathbreakers/1943a.html|archive-date=2015-08-25|url-status=dead}}</ref> Additionally, Ahn worked as an undergraduate research assistant in David Teller's lab, which investigated [[Hydrodynamic|protein hydrodynamics]], the study of the motion of proteins relative to their aqueous environment, which they can either be suspended or dissolved within.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Harding|first=Stephen|year=1999|title=Protein Hydrodynamics|url=https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/ncmh/documents/papers/paper216.pdf|journal=JAI|volume=2|pages=271–305}}</ref>

In 1985, she received her [[PhD]] in chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://biofrontiers.colorado.edu/about/directory/ahnn|title=Natalie Ahn|website=BioFrontiers Institute|publisher=University of Colorado|access-date=15 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170316102623/http://biofrontiers.colorado.edu/about/directory/ahnn|archive-date=16 March 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> Here, Ahn worked with Judith Klinman, studying [[enzymology]].<ref name=":4" />

Ahn's first postdoctoral job was studying hormone receptor binding at the University of Washington with Christoph de Haen.<ref name=":4" /> Ahn then moved to Edwin Kreb's lab, where she began her career in signal transduction.<ref name=":4" /> In this lab, Ahn was "one of the first to describe MAP kinases and MAP kinase kinases."<ref name=":4" /> She started working at the University of Colorado Boulder in 1992.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url = http://artsandsciences.colorado.edu/magazine/2013/04/following-the-pathways-to-metastatic-melanoma/|title = Following the Pathways to Metastatic Melanoma|date = 2013|access-date = 15 January 2016|website = Colorado Arts and Sciences Magazine|publisher = University of Colorado Boulder|last = Talbott|first = Clint|archive-date = 9 August 2013|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130809220255/http://artsandsciences.colorado.edu/magazine/2013/04/following-the-pathways-to-metastatic-melanoma/|url-status = dead}}</ref> Ahn was part of the [[Searle Scholars Program]] to fund young scientists' work in 1993.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|url = http://www.searlescholars.net/person/230|title = Natalie G. Ahn|access-date = 15 January 2016|website = Searle Scholars Program|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190326183403/https://www.searlescholars.net/person/230|archive-date = 26 March 2019|url-status = dead}}</ref> She was one of eight project collaborators who won a grant from the [[W. M. Keck Foundation|W.M. Keck Foundation]] for identifying [[protein]]s in a single cell type.<ref>{{Cite news|url = http://www.coloradanmagazine.org/2009/09/01/cu-people-september-2009/|title = CU People – September 2009|date = September 2009|work = Coloradan Magazine|access-date = 15 January 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100330020951/http://www.coloradanmagazine.org/2009/09/01/cu-people-september-2009/|archive-date = 30 March 2010|url-status = dead}}</ref> In 2012, she was named College Professor of Distinction at the University of Colorado.<ref name=":1" /> In 2014, she became part of the Subcellular Pan-Omics for Advanced Rapid Threat Assessment (SPARTA) team which is a biochemical project supported by the [[DARPA|Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency]] (DARPA).<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-358910897.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160911011334/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-358910897.html|url-status = usurped|archive-date = 11 September 2016|title = CU Awarded DARPA Cooperative Agreement to Assess Mechanisms of Drugs and Chemical Agents|date = 12 February 2014|work = Biotech Week|access-date = 15 January 2016|url-access = subscription|via = HighBeam Research }}</ref>

=== Current research ===
Ahn is currently working at the University of Colorado and is conducting research on cell signaling, information and proteomics, and molecular biophysics.<ref name=":4" /> Specific topics of her research include:
* Proteomics and Signal Transduction:
** The lab's goal is to investigate new mechanisms that are responsible for regulation and cell signaling.<ref name=":4" /> In order to do this, Ahn uses mass spectrometry for protein profiling in combination with biochemical and cellular approaches to better understand a cell's response to signaling pathways.
** In addition, Ahn investigates the internal motions of protein kinases, specifically studying their coupling protein dynamics and catalytic function.
** Ahn studies the development of cancer by examining "signaling pathways that are activated in melanoma and influence cancer progression and cell behavior."<ref name=":2" />
* Wnt5A signaling:
** Wnt5A is responsible for controlling embryonic body axis formation and can be found at high levels in melanomas, resulting in cell invasion. Ahn and her lab discovered the "Wnt5a receptor-actin-myosin-polarity (WRAMP) structure," which aids in directional cell movements by triggering membrane retraction. Ahn was able to determine WRAMP structure using organelle proteomics.<ref name=":2" />
* B-Raf signaling:
** In half of melanoma cells, the [[BRAF (gene)|B-Raf]] protein contains a missense mutation (V600E mutation), which is responsible for cell transformation, invasion, and metastasis. In order to profile phosphoproteins, Ahn uses [[Tandem mass spectrometry|negative precursor ion mass spectrometry]] to discover and count phosphopeptides. Ahn has identified numerous different proteins with this method and with this information studied how cell mechanisms used in cancer therapy were affected by protein-protein signaling.<ref name=":2" />
* Proteomics Technologies:
** In Ahn's lab, she uses multi dimensional liquid chromatography-MS/MS to identify over 8,000 proteins in each sequence of MS. Ahn's goal is to be more accurate and sensitive in these 2-D-LC-MS/MS techniques in assign proteins.<ref name=":2" />
* Protein Kinase Dynamics:
** In Ahn's lab, she uses hydrogen-exchange mass spectrometry (HX-MS) to discover and better understand protein motions on the inside of kinases, where energy fluctuations occur. Ahn's goal is to understand how the different protein dynamics are able to regulate catalytic activity in specific enzymes, most notably protein kinase. Ahn conducts research which focuses on ERK2 MAP kinases, that provide an ideal model due to their clear link between activity and protein dynamics.<ref name=":9" />

=== Community service ===
Ahn was elected president of the [[American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology]] (ASBMB) in the summer of 2015.<ref name=":4" /> She was previously a member of the council.<ref name=":4" /> She began attending the ASBMB annual meeting while still a PhD student at the University of California, Berkeley and gave her first public research talk at one of these meetings.<ref name=":4" />
